newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Debt pledge clears Russian Eurobond hurdle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Debt pledge clears Russian Eurobond hurdle.

text.p: A top Russian official said on Friday that commercial banks were set to reschedule billions of dollars of Soviet-era debts, paving the way for the first Eurobond issue for Russia as a sovereign borrower.
Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov told Reuters that commercial banks had agreed in principle to reschedule more than $20 billion of the debts Russia inherited when the Soviet Union fell apart.
This opens the door to the rescheduling all of the $35 billion Russia owes the banks.

"By preliminary estimates the amount of debt declared by the banks agreeing to take part exceeds $20 billion of the principal," he said. "We can announce today that the agreement will take place before the end of this year."
Russian debt prices soared on the news.

"It's still cheap. I'd buy all the way up to the Eurobond issue, then sell," UBS analyst Alex Mitcheson-Smith said in London after the price of Russian Vneshekonombank debt rose to 66-1/4 cents to the dollar.
The price of Russian debt has more than doubled since the start of this year.
Russian shares were also firmer and dollar-denominated Ministry of Finance bonds rose to new highs.
The agreement with the so-called London Club of commercial banks gives the green light for the issue of Russia's first Eurobond, giving it a chance for getting an investment grade credit rating.

Kasyanov said Russia planned to issue the Eurobond at the end of October or start of November. Officials had earlier said Russia would issue a $300-$500 million Eurobond in late September or early October.
"It is not a postponement, it's the schedule we worked out in May," Kasyanov said.
U.S. rating agencies have already been drawing up ratings for Russia and officials in Moscow say they are satisfied with the way the rating process is going.
Kasyanov said rating results could be announced in a week.

If Russia does not reschedule its $35 billion debt to the London Club and $40 billion debt to the Paris Club of government creditors, Moscow may get a poor rating, which would exclude pension funds from a list of potential buyers.
Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, which chairs the bank advisory committee on Russian debt, said in a statement that proposals for the rescheduling had been well received.

Kasyanov said the former Soviet foreign trade bank Vneshekonombank, which is responsible for debt payments, would need another week to check the details of the agreement with the banks. A final deal would take a futher two months.
Russia in June agreed with the London Club to reschedule $25 billion in principal and over $7 billion in interest arrears.
Separately, the Paris Club agreed this April to reschedule its part of former Soviet debt for up to 25 years, including a grace period of six years.
Russian officials are meeting individual members of the Paris Club to negotiate rescheduling of debts owed to them.
A draft of the 1997 budget said Russia planned to raise a total $1.3 billion in Eurobonds next year.
